title: Complex Numbers

notes.heading: 1. Conjugate, Modulus, Principal Argument & Euler Form
notes.proseLatex: Every complex number $z = x + iy$ ($x,y\in\mathbb{R}$, $i^2 = -1$) has conjugate $\bar{z} = x - iy$ and modulus $|z| = \sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ satisfying $z\bar{z} = |z|^2$ and $z^{-1} = \bar{z}/|z|^2$. Its principal argument $\theta = \operatorname{Arg}(z) \in (-\pi, \pi]$ must be adjusted by quadrant: $\alpha$ in Q-I, $\pi-\alpha$ in Q-II, $-(\pi-\alpha)$ in Q-III, and $-\alpha$ in Q-IV where $\alpha = \arctan(|y/x|)$. Euler's form $z = r e^{i\theta} = r(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)$ turns multiplication and division into addition and subtraction of arguments.

keyFormulas.label: Modulus, Conjugate & Euler Representation
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Convert complex fractions into modulus and argument operations.

keyFormulas.label: Triangle Inequality Bounds
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Find maximum and minimum modulus of shifted complex loci.

examples.problemLatex: Find the modulus and principal argument of $z = -1 + i\sqrt{3}$.
stepsLatex: Point $(-1, \sqrt{3})$ lies in Quadrant II with reference angle $\alpha = \arctan(\sqrt{3}/1) = \pi/3$, so $\operatorname{Arg}(z) = \pi - \pi/3 = 2\pi/3$.

notes.heading: 2. De Moivre's Theorem & Cube Roots of Unity
notes.proseLatex: For any integer $n$ (and as one branch for rational $n$), $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos(n\theta) + i\sin(n\theta)$. Solving $z^3 = 1$ gives $1, \omega, \omega^2$ where $\omega = -\frac{1}{2} + i\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = e^{i2\pi/3}$, governed by the twin identities $\omega^3 = 1$ and $1 + \omega + \omega^2 = 0$. Powers $i^m$ repeat modulo $4$ ($i^{4k+r} = i^r$) while $\omega^m$ repeats modulo $3$ ($\omega^{3k+r} = \omega^r$).

keyFormulas.label: De Moivre's Theorem & Cube Roots of Unity
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Simplify high powers of complex expressions and omega cyclic sums.

examples.problemLatex: Evaluate $(1 - \omega + \omega^2)(1 + \omega - \omega^2)$ where $\omega \neq 1$ is a cube root of unity.

notes.heading: 3. Argand Plane Loci (Circles, Bisectors & Rays)
notes.proseLatex: Geometrically, $|z - z_0| = R$ represents a circle of centre $z_0$ and radius $R$, whereas $|z - z_1| = |z - z_2|$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining $z_1$ and $z_2$. When $\left|\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}\right| = k$ ($k>0, k\neq 1$), the locus is an Apollonius circle; and purely imaginary $\frac{z - z_1}{z - z_2}$ ($\arg = \pm\pi/2$) traces the circle having $z_1 z_2$ as diameter (excluding $z_2$).

keyFormulas.label: Standard Argand Loci
keyFormulas.latex: $|z - z_0| = R \text{ (circle)};\quad |z - z_1| = |z - z_2| \text{ (perp. bisector)};\quad \operatorname{Re}\!\left(\frac{z-z_1}{z-z_2}\right)=0 \text{ (diameter circle)}$
keyFormulas.aiExplainContext: Identify geometric locus directly without expanding x + iy.

wbjeebTraps: Quadrant sign trap: $\operatorname{Arg}(-1 - i)$ is $-3\pi/4$, NOT $\pi/4$ (raw $\arctan((-1)/(-1)) = \pi/4$ misses Quadrant III).
Inequality $z_1 < z_2$ is meaningless for non-real complex numbers — only moduli $|z_1| < |z_2|$ can be ordered.
Check $\left(\frac{1+i}{1-i}\right) = i$ and $\left(\frac{1-i}{1+i}\right) = -i$ first before expanding high powers like $\left(\frac{1+i}{1-i}\right)^{100} = i^{100} = 1$.
